newsitem.title: USA: BOXING-JAPAN PREPARED TO SAY 'NO' TO TYSON.
newsitem.headline: BOXING-JAPAN PREPARED TO SAY 'NO' TO TYSON.

text.p: Former champion Mike Tyson will not be allowed to fight in Japan if he is suspended from boxing by the Nevada State Athletic Commission, but other countries have yet to follow suit, a U.S. boxing official said Wednesday.

"I understand that Japan has talked to us and they would follow our lead but other countries have not done as yet so I think that Mr. Tyson could fight (in other countries)", said Luther Mack, a member of the Nevada State Athletic Commission, in a television interview with ABC's "Good Morning America."

The commission was holding a disciplinary hearing later Wednesday over Tyson's ear-biting incident in a title fight on June 28 against champion Evander Holyfield. Tyson was disqualified after biting both of Holyfield's ears in the third round.
The five-man commission temporarily suspended Tyson last week and froze his $30 million purse for the fight.
Under current rules, the commission, which regulates boxing in Nevada, could suspend Tyson, fine him or revoke his boxing license and withhold up to 10 percent of his purse.
Mack said if Tyson is fined, the money would go to a "general fund" in Nevada for government programmes.

Under new federal laws, a suspension in Nevada could effectively bar Tyson from fighting anywhere in the United States. The law does not force other states to honour a Nevada ban, but those states would have to justify allowing him to fight.

The last time Tyson fought in Japan was February 1990, when he suffered his only other defeat in the ring, a knockout in Tokyo by James "Buster" Douglas in one of the biggest upsets in boxing history.
